en: The Cyprus Mines Corporation was founded on the strength of the Roman tailings, which told Gunther where to dig. Modern Cypriot mining and much of the island's twentieth-century economy grew from an archaeological observation.

The largest asbestos mine in Europe, cut into the serpentine of the Troodos above 1,100 metres. Working began in 1904 when an Italian bought the licence from the British administration, and over the life of the mine roughly 130 million tonnes of rock were moved to win about a million tonnes of chrysotile fibre from ore grading barely one per cent. It closed in 1988, leaving a grey scar visible from the far side of the island and a legacy of asbestos disease among its workers. Rehabilitation began in 1995 and is expected to run to 2030; it is the largest environmental restoration project on Cyprus.

en: A stavropegic monastery at about 870 m on the north flank of the Machairas range, founded by the hermits Neophytos and Ignatios who, tradition says, found an icon of the Virgin in a cave in 1145 and had to cut their way to it with a knife, machaira, which gave the house its name. Ignatios went to Constantinople in 1172 and came back with the endowment of Manuel I Komnenos, the whole mountain and independence from the local bishop. The monk Neilos enlarged it in the early thirteenth century and wrote its typikon. It burned in 1892 and everything standing is later, but it is the best surviving example of a great Byzantine foundation that kept its independence through three centuries of Latin rule.

en: A small Turkish Cypriot coastal village in the Tillyria that became the most fought-over point of the 1963 to 1964 crisis, because it was the one beach through which men and weapons could reach the Turkish Cypriot fighters from Turkey. en: On 11 July 2011 ninety-eight containers of gunpowder and ammunition, seized in 2009 from the Cypriot-flagged ship Monchegorsk carrying Iranian material towards Syria and then left stacked in the open at the Evangelos Florakis naval base, caught fire and exploded. An independent inquiry found that President Christofias bore primary responsibility; the defence minister, the foreign minister and the National Guard commander resigned.

en: The red villages of the south-east, named for the terra rossa soil that makes their potatoes, are the clearest case of the island's central modern problem: there is not enough water. Cyprus answered with dams, then with desalination, and in the drought of 2008 with tankers of drinking water from Greece. The 1974 line also runs along the top of the district, cutting these villages off from Famagusta, their market town.
